newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS - Brazil seed tightness threatens yield.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS - Brazil seed tightness threatens yield.

text.p: Low domestic availability of certified quality soybean seeds for Brazil's forthcoming planting season is pushing seed prices sky-high and could lead to imports, seed producers and analysts said.
In addition, crop productivity could suffer, they said.

"In 1996, certified seed availability will fall to 750,000 tonnes, down from 840,000 tonnes in 1995 and some 900,000 - one million tonnes a year up to 1994," said Joao Henrique Hummel, executive director of the Brazilian Seed Producers' Association.
"The expected lower usage of certified seeds this year will reduce crop productivity, as non-certified seeds respond less favorably to fertiliser," he said.
In the 1995/96 crop planting, Brazil used 1.3 million tonnes of seeds, of which around 65 percent were certified, the association director said.

Certification is gained following testing according to Ministry of Agriculture norms, and certified seeds are normally resistant to the soybean diseases which can occur in the states of Goias, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and Parana, he said.
The rest of the seeds used for planting in the last harvest were soybeans from storage which were of lower quality, he said.

Certified seed availability has fallen because of factors including producers' limited cash flow and high interest rates, Hummel said. Around 480 companies specialise in seed production in Brazil, he said.
Brazil's 1996/97 soybean planting season is due to start in October. Trade in seeds is now hotting up, partly due to the reduced availability of certified seeds, Hummel said.

In addition, seed demand should be greater this year due to soybean producers' intentions to plant an area five to ten percent larger than last year, encouraged by favorable international soybean prices.

Brazil's next soybean harvest may be back to 1994/95 levels of 26 million tonnes but won't be much bigger than that because of the current seed supply and pricing problems," said analyst Carlos Cogo of Agromercados.
"But it should be greater than 1995/96's 23 million tonnes," he said.
In Rio Grande do Sul state, certified seeds are currently being sold for 22 reais ($21.57) per 50 kilo bag, up from some 14 reais (approx $14.74) a year ago, Hummel said.
In Mato Grosso state, certified seeds are fetching 32 reais ($31.37) a bag, over double the price of a year ago.
Cogo said that seeds normally cost between 50-75 percent more than soybeans in Brazil.
Given the current demand for seeds, and rising soybean prices, it can be supposed most seed transactions will be made at 75 percent above soybean prices in the near future, he said.
The analyst said that given the local demand, seeds may have to be imported into Brazil this year.

"If imports occur, the whole market will change," he said. "It's a very delicate subject right now. There's a lot of pressure from seed producing sources not to import as this would bring prices right down."

Domestic soybean prices meanwhile continued their upwards climb this week. The national soybean price, a composite average, jumped up to $16.31 a 60-kilo bag on Sept 5, up from $15.93 the day before and $15.16 a week previously.
Trade sources reported crushers Sadia and Perdigao acquired soybeans for 18.10 reais ($17.74) a 60-kilo bag in Rio Grande do Sul state and 18.08 reais ($17.72) a bag in Santa Catarina.

In Brazil's centrewest, rural product bond (CPR) advance soybean sales were reported at 9 reais ($8.82) a 60-kilo bag, considerably higher than the 5 reais ($4.9) traditional for CPR sales in that area.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
